https://english.republika.mk/world/orban.text: Overt tyranny has arrived in Hugary, said former Prime Minister Viktor Orban after the latest round of powergrab moves by Petar Magyar, who is forcing the President of the country Tamas Sulyok to resign. Magyar and his Tisza party carried out an unprecedented attack on the President, putting him in an undignified position and removed him from office. This has not happened in Hungary since the days of the darkest dictatorship. Sulyok is a victim of political violence. If you can do this to a President, there is no end to what you can do to an individual citizen. May God protect Hungary, said Orban. Tisza has a majority sufficient to amend the Constitution and is using it to force officials who are not loyal to the party out of office. https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-a.text: Russian airstrikes across Ukraine have killed at least 12 people and injured dozens more in multiple drone and missile attacks overnight, according to local authorities. The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched six missiles and 151 attack drones throughout Friday night, hitting 12 locations. Ukrainian authorities managed to down 135 drones. The attacks came as Ukraine continues to urge Western allies to provide more air defense systems and interceptor missiles. Advertisement Advertisement President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the drone attacks killed three people — a 3-year-old child and the child’s grandparents — in a village in the Kyiv region. The six ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, killing one person, he said. “More pressure is needed. New sanctions that will prevent the production of these ballistic missiles,” Zelenskyy said on X. “And we definitely need more protection for our people,” he added, appealing to allies to provide missile interceptors to strengthen Ukraine’s defenses against Russia’s aerial assault. In the Zaporizhzhia region, in southeast Ukraine, three people were killed and four were wounded following the overnight attack, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said . A further five people were killed and nearly 50 people wounded in the regions of Kharkiv , Donetsk and Kherson , according to regional authorities. Separately, Zelenskyy visited Serbia on Saturday — his first trip to the country since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine — to meet with President Aleksandar Vučić and Prime Minister Đuro Macut. Zelenskyy said the talks had focused on rebuilding infrastructure, readying a free-trade agreement this year, and preparing for the winter to come. This article has been updated. https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/.text: Philstar.com HOME Headlines Opinion Nation World Business Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Events Other Sections The Philippine Star Pilipino Star Ngayon HOME Bansa Metro Probinsiya Opinyon Palaro Showbiz True Confessions Dr. Love Litra-talk Kutob Komiks The Freeman HOME Cebu News Opinion Metro Cebu Region Cebu Business Cebu Sports Cebu Lifestyle Cebu Entertainment Pang-Masa HOME Police Metro Punto Mo Pang Movies PM Sports Para Manalo Para Malibang Banat HOME Balita Opinyon Kalingawan Showbiz Palaro Imong Kapalaran Punsoy Interaksyon HOME Trends + Spotlights Politics + Issues Celebrities Hobbies + Interests Rumor Cop Coupons HOME Top Stores Offers By Category Latest Posts SARA ON TRIAL SONA 2026 DUTERTE AT ICC FUEL PRICE TRACKER INFLUENCE OPS EXPLAINERS FACT CHECKS ENVIRONMENT My Profile Sign Out HOME HEADLINES OPINION NATION WORLD BUSINESS SPORTS ENTERTAINMENT LIFESTYLE EVENTS COUPONS OTHER SECTIONS Headlines Lithuania eyes sharing Ukraine-tested maritime tech with PCG MANILA, Philippines — Lithuania is looking to bring maritime security technologies emerging from the war in Ukraine to the Philippine Coast Guard, Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said, part of a widening security partnership between the two countries. Budrys said he discussed the technologies with PCG officials during a July 23 visit to the service's headquarters in Manila, describing them as systems that would make the coast guard's work easier. "I had a really good exchange with the Philippine Coast Guard on some technologies that would make their work — important work for the international community — easier," Budrys told Philstar.com in an interview on July 23. "We are talking about some technologies that ... concern the protection of the sea routes," he added. The Lithuanian minister noted that Russia's war in Ukraine has become the main driver of development in the defense industry and in dual-use technologies. "We have to use everything that we see is developing so fast in Ukraine, in their efforts and brave efforts to defend themselves, and also turn those technologies — the usable ones — in the peacetime for our own good," he said. Beyond maritime hardware, Budrys said Vilnius is offering "niche" high-tech capabilities, particularly in cybersecurity. The PCG said in a statement Monday that both sides agreed to establish a technical working group to explore cooperation in cybersecurity, professional training, and marine environmental protection, among others. Lithuania denounces Chinese vessels' behavior Budrys' visit comes amid heightened tensions in the West Philippine Sea. Lithuania has been among the most outspoken European critics of both Russian aggression and Chinese coercion, particularly after facing Beijing’s trade boycotts over its ties with Taiwan. Prior to his meeting with the PCG, Budrys told Philstar.com he had been closely following the reported incidents of harassment faced by the Coast Guard in the West Philippine Sea. On the day of Budrys's visit, the PCG had reported the China Coast Guard's (CCG) use of water cannons on Philippine vessels conducting a humanitarian fuel subsidy mission near Scarborough Shoal. Two days earlier, the PCG reported that CCG personnel had physically clubbed a Navy serviceman near Ayungin Shoal. "We were following the incidents that were happening in the West Philippine Sea, with the vessels that were acting under different covers of the civilian vessels coming from China," he told Philstar.com . "Those developments were really disturbing and [something] that all of the international community has to have its position on." He called the incidents breaches of international law and of UNCLOS. Budrys also drew a parallel with the Baltic Sea, where Lithuania and its neighbors have reported repeated damage to undersea cables and power links. At least eleven cables in the Baltic region have been severed or damaged since October 2023, caused by incidents of shadow vessels dragging their anchors across the seabed, making criminal intent difficult to prove under maritime law. "Those affected countries have to share their experience and ways on how to protect ourselves within international law, even understanding that the other side is not respecting it," Budrys said, warning that compromises in one theater threaten global stability. "If we cannot apply it here, why should it be applied somewhere else — for example, in the Strait of Hormuz?" he added. Lithuania was among 14 nations that recently marked the 10th anniversary of the 2016 South China Sea arbitral award — the landmark Hague decision that invalidated China’s expansive claims — reaffirming that the ruling remains legally binding. China's foreign ministry rejected the statement, which it said "disregards the basic facts of the South China Sea." The Philippines and Lithuania last year signed a defense cooperation agreement that included a focus on cyber- and maritime security. https://www.politico.eu/article/eppo-eur.text: A budgetary squeeze and bureaucratic inertia threaten the future of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, its top official told POLITICO. In a wide-ranging interview, Laura Codruța Kövesi, who wraps up her seven-year tenure on Friday, said: “As I leave my office, I think of this famous Danish TV show Borgen. There is a very famous saying there: ‘In Brussels, no one can hear you scream,’ and unfortunately, this is true,” she said, in a nod to the Ridley Scott blockbuster Alien. “I am concerned that the EPPO is going to be killed softly because it’s doing its job,” she added in blunt remarks about justice in Europe. Advertisement Advertisement Kövesi also discussed her interactions with the EU institutions, Greece’s farm subsidy scandal and questions of national sovereignty in the interview, which took place via video call from her office in Luxembourg. This transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Your term concludes this week, so what were the main difficulties during your term and what could should happen in a different way by your successor? When I was appointed, I promised that I would build an efficient, strong and independent institution, which citizens will trust. I think we managed, together with my colleagues, to do this to a large extent. I’m aware that we didn’t succeed in everything, but no one can dispute that we did a good job. The most important question now is whether this continues. I listened to all the candidates for the European Chief Prosecutor and I was really worried, because one candidate presented himself saying that his project was to normalize EPPO. For someone like me, growing up during communism, this is very threatening. Another candidate, even worse, spoke about maintaining equal distance between the prosecution office and all the political parties. But how will this be compatible with an independent office? After the first years of activity, we have results that only few people expected. We have a lot of reactions, and I think we have proved the law is equal for everybody. Now the key challenge for the EPPO and especially for my successor will be to keep the EPPO independent and credible. Advertisement Advertisement What has surprised you most during those this term? The last seven years was the toughest job that I have ever had. I didn’t have a lot of surprises. But I have to tell you about the attacks or attempts to undermine our independence. The most blatant attempt to intimidate EPPO happened in Greece, where we had this issue with the renewal of the European delegated prosecutors. The main challenge of the EPPO will be this one: the revision of regulation. It is clear that this will show who is a true friend of an independent judiciary. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office’s logo is seen at its headquarters in Luxembourg on June 1, 2021. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images The second example was an attack against our credibility. Everybody knows that we are drowning under work, and I understand that there are many priorities, but we have to see whether this is real or is this just a pretext. Here the surprise comes from Poland. We agreed that we need 24 European delegated prosecutors. The expectations were huge, and our credibility is at stake. In this moment, we have only 15. So how can we be credible in Poland? In Hungary, also, we explained exactly what budget we need to do our job, but the Commission proposed half of what we need. These are few examples how you can, if you want, destroy the credibility of an institution. As I leave my office, I think of this famous Danish TV show Borgen. There is a very famous saying there: “In Brussels, no one can hear you scream,” and unfortunately, this is true. I am concerned that the EPPO is going to be killed softly because it’s doing its job. You mentioned pressure from local governments, particularly from Greece and Poland. Was there any support from the EU institutions? Advertisement Advertisement We had support of different stakeholders in some cases, but when I say that I’m concerned that EPPO is going to be killed softly for doing its job, I have three main reasons. It’s easy, it’s a pattern. If you want to destroy an institution, you can do three things, that are happening now. First, you are underfunded. On paper we should have 230 European delegated prosecutors, and we have money only for 180. We have money for only one third of what security service costs, and I would have endless examples. Second, a lot of delays. Since 2021, we said that the revision of the EPPO regulation has to start earlier. It’s delayed. Thirdly, I have learned that here everything is complicated — and I thought that Romania is complicated. To give you an example, there are these endless discussions about anti-fraud architecture. We discovered a new continent of crime, and we see the criminal organizations are growing, defrauding the EU budget and national budgets. In the middle of this, should be the fight against organized criminality. Instead, we have endless discussion about how to complicate the life of the prosecutors, and we discuss a lot about this joint intake registry. If there is money to have this new registry electronically, how is it possible that money doesn’t exist for what we really need? Do you feel that you have managed to shake things up? Have people or institutions started behaving differently? A lot of changes happened due to the EPPO. The level of detection increased in most of the member states, the level of successful cases increased, and obviously the protection of the EU budget is higher with the EPPO. But still, there are things that are not working the way they should be. If you had the chance to do it all over again, what is the main thing that you would do differently? Nothing. I would do the same things, but maybe the others should change their behavior. I thought that there is a big difference between Brussels and what I saw in Romania. But in Romania, or other member states, people are used to work with prosecutors, they know what the prosecutors are doing. Advertisement Advertisement In Brussels, sometimes at EU level, they think that they are above the law, and this for me is a problem. In Romania, or other member states, if you are called in for a statement, you show up, because you know that you have to do this. Here, sometimes there is this feeling that you are above the prosecutors, you are above the law, and you don’t come. Some prosecutors that could be politically motivated, are in a position to delay the outcome of cases, postpone hearings, meetings. Have you experienced that in some countries more than others? All our European delegated prosecutors are very independent, and our agenda is not based on any electoral campaign or other interests than what is written in our regulation. There are some cases that can be delayed, but this is not because the prosecutors do not want to do their job. EU flags fly outside the European Commission’s Berlaymont building in Brussels on Feb. 17, 2025. | Thierry Monasse/Getty Images Some politicians think that they are above the law, and if you are called in for a statement, you have to come, and it’s not all the time the same understanding. So, this is an example in which the prosecutors cannot finalize the cases. Do you refer to Pfizergate? I will not comment anything on specific investigations. Advertisement Advertisement You have noted in your reports that the reporting rate from EU institutions has been minimal. Are there instances where they saw corruption cases and they haven’t reported it back? When I started, I heard that we are a clean country, and we don’t have corruption. And I said many times that there is no clean country. But with the EPPO, this has changed a lot. But I will not be shy to tell you, that especially when important people are involved in the investigation — be it high-profile politicians or rich people who are connected to the political class — we have difficulties in exercising our competence because we still have this issue of conflict of competences. Unfortunately, we witness situations in which, when we have opened an investigation and when we were ready to have different measures in our investigation, suddenly on national level, a case with the same object was opened, and the general prosecutor decided that we are not competent to investigate the case. And this is something that affects the capabilities and the capacity of EPPO to make investigations. In several countries the argument against cooperating with the EPPO is that they would be eliminating their country’s sovereignty. How do you respond to that? Is it better to have the sovereignty of criminals? Because this is what you have to put in balance. The criminal organizations in Europe are not national anymore, and they take advantage of this fragmentation that exists. Advertisement We are still applying the national legislation; we are still going in front of the national court. I don’t think you lose your sovereignty; you win more protection and more security for your citizens. Is it better to let the criminals operate freely, to take advantage of the fragmentation, to take advantage that no one has a helicopter view to see how they operate on the entire territory of the EU? In Greece some politicians say that they could simply stop working with the EPPO. Can a country that joined the EPPO simply pull out? Well, I don’t know if they want to go out of the European Union or not, but to go out from EPPO, it’s almost impossible. These kinds of comments don’t do anything else than to prove exactly what I said. There will be attempts to kill the EPPO because we do our job. Farmers participate in a protest over delays in European compensation payments, in Nikaia, Greece on Dec. 4, 2025. | Thanasis Kaliakoudas/SOOC/AFP via Getty Images Some politicians speak about an independent and efficient judiciary, until you touch them and until you go close to their inner circle. In that moment, the prosecutors are abusive, they have a political agenda, they are not needed. After that, they start to try to diminish your competence, to let you without money, to dismantle the specialized police. There are currently cases being investigated in several countries involving political figures or parties, like the OPEKEPE farm scandal in Greece or in France . These countries have elections soon and the EPPO is criticized for being politically motivated. How do you make sure that there is an outcome in all these cases that doesn’t coincide with elections? You mentioned OPEKEPE, we just finalized some indictments there. The cases are in court. But all the noise was created to blame EPPO that we play politics instead of discussing what happened in reality. You have politicians who want to cover the discussion, try to undermine the credibility of EPPO. You come and you create a smoke. Oh, we will have elections. Look what the EPPO is doing. Advertisement If you ask EPPO to abstain and to not do anything because there are elections in Europe, we will not work at all. And our job is not to check when the electoral campaign is, but to check if the honest farmers have access to EU money. Instead, the money was allocated to different people who pretended they are farmers and used the money to go in fancy trips and have luxurious cars, and the honest farmers didn’t get anything. I don’t see any links between what we did, our activity, our cases, and electoral campaigns. The only connection is when you have some unhappy politicians, they want to attack EPPO, and they try to intimidate and stop us from doing our job. The integrity of the OPEKEPE investigation was questioned here in Greece after a case file was sent to Parliament for lifting the immunity of 11 MPs. Eventually, only four of these were sent to court, and there was criticism it was done hastily. Was something done wrong there? No, nothing went wrong from our perspective. When we ask for the lifting the immunity, it’s not about the guilt. It’s just a condition to allow the prosecutors to make the investigation and to gather evidences. What are your personal plans for the future? Well, let’s not speak about my personal plans. Let’s focus on the EPPO. I will see after I finish my mandate.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: The Markley Lowell datacentre in Lowell, Massachusetts. The US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. Photograph: Lauren Owens Lambert/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Markley Lowell datacentre in Lowell, Massachusetts. The US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. Photograph: Lauren Owens Lambert/AFP/Getty Images Datacentres Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent Thu 19 Nov 2026 00.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog. The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth. The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain. Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history. “I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol. Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said. View image in fullscreen A datacentre under construction at the Google Storey County campus in Sparks, Nevada, US. Photograph: Daniel Cole/Reuters Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China. By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants. In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union. As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said. The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said. This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power. View image in fullscreen Workers at TikTok’s datacentre in Hamar, Norway. Photograph: Victoria Klesty/Reuters The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world. Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said. The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres. https://telex.hu/english/2026/11/26/why-.text: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky held their first official meeting in Transcarpathia this week. At the press conference held following the meeting, it was mentioned that-as expected-the subject of Ukrainian corn was also discussed during the visit. Péter Magyar said that the two countries’ ministers of agriculture would soon be holding talks on Hungary importing corn from Ukraine, while Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine might be able to supply "certain quantities" of corn to Hungary, as they are aware that this year’s harvest had been low. It may seem like the subject of Ukrainian corn has little impact on the daily lives of Hungarians, but it is in fact crucial for the entire Hungarian food industry. Among other things, corn shortage poses a threat to Hungary’s production of isoglucose, alcohol, and animal feed-all of which are competitive at the European level-and, through the latter, to cattle and pig farming as well as dairy production. Not only is there a risk of price increases, but also of shortage in general: after all, there can be no finished products without raw materials. Nevertheless, this is a highly divisive subject in Hungary. As we shall see, there is strong opposition to importing Ukrainian corn within the Fidesz camp, largely due to the desire to protect Hungarian farmers, opposition to GMOs, and concerns about alleged contamination, while Tisza voters-although they do share some of the same concerns-are much more likely to attribute the ban to Fidesz’s anti-Ukrainian stance. Most of them would support the import of Ukrainian grain because of the expected lower retail prices and the ability to better supply the food processing industry. The agricultural sector has traditionally lined up on both sides of the issue, with field crop farmers opposed to importing Ukrainian grain because they fear competition will drive down prices. A significant portion of the Hungarian economy, however-livestock farmers, feed producers, and industrial processors-firmly believe that keeping Ukrainian grain out would be self-defeating and would create serious problems for the country's economy. Magyar Mezőgazdaság summarized the situation across Europe, based on data from a Polish study. In 2026, corn production in the EU fell to just 50.2 million metric tons, a nearly 20-year low; the average yield over the previous 10 years was 61.3 million metric tons. Climate change-more specifically, drought and heat-is clearly to blame. Under such circumstances, the role of imports naturally increases, while the fact that one of the key starting points for imports-namely, Ukrainian shipments departing via the Black Sea destined for Spain, Italy, and France, among other countries-has become unreliable due to Russian attacks, hasn't helped the situation. The dry, hot weather caused the biggest losses in Hungary, France, Romania, and Germany. Due to the weaker European harvest, imports may reach a record 23.5 million metric tons, and Ukraine has traditionally been the most important supplier on the seller’s side of EU imports. Due to logistical costs, it is rather unfortunate that the next countries on the list are the United States and Brazil. The biggest importers of corn in the EU were Spain, the Netherlands, and Italy. These countries purchase several million metric tons of Ukrainian corn annually. In Hungary, corn shortage has affected the feed and processing industries the most. The Hungarian figures are well known: According to Zoltán Reng, CEO of Hungrana Starch and Isoglucose Manufacturing Ltd. (Hungrana Keményítő- és Izocukorgyártó Kft.)-one of Europe’s leading corn processors-this year’s corn harvest was exceptionally low in Hungary, totaling just 1.4 to 1.5 million metric tons. Meeting domestic demand would require at least 1.7–2 million metric tons of imports, even with certain sectors striving to utilize all available substitute products. According to the Grain Association (Gabonaszövetség), securing 800,000 metric tons remains unresolved. This was also confirmed to us by Zoltán Reng. According to him, while there indeed are other sources of corn in Poland, Slovakia, and Romania, the logistics of importing them remains unresolved-there simply isn’t enough transportation capacity via rail or road, nor are there enough proper transshipment facilities. Germany, the Netherlands, and France are now also competing for these goods, which has created a “first come, first served” sort of situation. Utilizing additional road and rail capacity from Ukraine would be possible, especially since the Ukrainians are heavily dependent on rail exports to Europe because-as previously mentioned, they are unable to use their maritime capacity. In other words, there is a classic balance of supply and demand, but due to existing Hungarian regulations, we are unable to import. In our background interviews, we heard that while the Ministry of Agriculture is aware of the problem, proposals to relax existing regulations have not yet been approved by the Tisza government’s top leadership. Professional consultations are, of course, ongoing. It is interesting to note that even former Central Bank Governor György Surányi has addressed this self-inflicted economic hardship in his presentation on evaluating the budget. According to Zsombor Wagenhoffer, director of the Hungarian Livestock Breeders’ Association (Magyar Állattenyésztők Szövetsége), the problem stems from the fact that domestic corn production used to be around 6.5 million metric tons annually, which consistently placed Hungary among the top five exporters in Europe. In response to the abundant supply, several processing plants sprang up, but then the trend reversed, and the lean years began. Livestock farmers are now faced with a situation where all feed is expensive, while the prices of end products (beef, pork, poultry) have plummeted. Feed accounts for 50–70 percent of the costs in livestock farming, so this greatly affects profitability. According to Wagenhoffer, shielding an entire sector (crop farmers) from European competition is not possible, especially not while putting other sectors (livestock farmers) at a disadvantage—all while watching Spanish-raised pigs, fattened on Ukrainian grain, drive Hungarian farmers out of business. To make matters worse, due to the drought, a considerable percentage of Hungarian grain is contaminated with toxins. The most serious risk associated with corn in the EU is aflatoxin: it occurs naturally as a fungal toxin (mycotoxin), and is produced by certain types of mold. Heat and drought contribute to a sharp increase in contamination. Livestock farmers still have some stockpiles, but these may run out towards the beginning of next year, at which point they will need to purchase corn immediately. However, since the harvest was also down in Ukraine, countries without import restrictions could end up buying their entire export quota of 10–20 million metric tons. The government would like everyone to compromise, but the price is a major concern for crop farmers. They argue, among other things, that Ukrainian produce is uncertified and of poor quality, and that “Hungary is an agricultural nation” capable of producing what it needs. Another argument is that Ukrainian grain is the product of a large American-Ukrainian agribusiness lobby. Farmers are not the only ones who have been making these claims in recent years. Fidesz also managed to persuade the public that Ukrainian grain is of poor quality, will ruin Hungarian farmers with its low prices, and is genetically modified. As things stand, it seems that no matter how popular the Tisza Party is, it does not dare speak out against the messages Fidesz drilled into the public consciousness: lower utility bills for everyone, keep Ukrainian grain out, and curb inflation through pricing regulations. Another reason why continuing with the policy of banning Ukrainian grain is hard to understand-even though Péter Magyar sometimes speaks out against “EU funds being freely handed out to Ukraine” and considers MOL’s fuel storage facility on the country's eastern border rather risky-is that bilateral meetings have begun, there have been gestures of goodwill, and Ukraine has also taken some steps, for example, in the area of minority rights. So let us take a look at the figures mentioned above! According to a survey conducted by the 21 Research Center (21 Kutatóközpont) via telephone, Hungarians are divided on the issue of Ukrainian grain imports, and their opinions are in a correlation with their party preferences. The survey was commissioned by chemical engineer László Rácz and was conducted by telephone with 1,000 respondents in the final days of September 2026. According to the survey, Fidesz voters are primarily worried about the quality of Ukrainian grain and the interests of Hungarian farmers; as a result, most of them would still not allow Ukrainian grain imports. Tisza voters tend to suspect that Fidesz's ban on Ukrainian grain imports was driven by political motives, anti-Ukrainian sentiment, and propaganda, and they believe that the move has led to higher food prices. Most of them would allow imports, although they, too, typically express concern for Hungarian farmers. Seventy percent of Hungarians have heard there is a grain shortage in the country, and 85 percent are aware that the Fidesz government banned Ukrainian grain imports in 2023. Respondents were also asked about why this was done; the most frequently cited answers were the protection of domestic farmers (14 percent) and genetic modification (14 percent), Ukraine’s lack of compliance with EU standards (12 percent), with several respondents citing food safety (11 percent) and political reasons (11 percent), while anti-Ukrainian sentiment (10 percent) was also mentioned. Overall, more people are opposed to importing grain from Ukraine (51 percent) than would allow it (42 percent). Political affiliation played a very strong role on this issue: the overwhelming majority of Fidesz supporters-87 percent-would not allow such imports, while the majority of Tisza supporters (65 percent) would. Processors argue that, when it comes to corn imports, the government shouldn't necessarily consider opening the market entirely if it deems this to be politically risky. Rather, this could be a temporary, quantitatively limited, and strictly controlled system designed to make up for the confirmed domestic shortfall-for example, based on transparent quotas tied to actual usage. The question is, whether farmers would accept that opening the market might also be in their best interest? It seemed to us that they would not-or at least not everyone would. This is likely so because devising a mechanism that would prevent imports from flooding the market, one that would ensure that imports only enter the scene once Hungarian products were sold out is quite difficult. And yet, the longer-term stakes of this subject could very well have an impact on the farmers too. If domestic livestock farming and the processing industry experience a permanent loss of capacity due to the current shortage of raw materials, Hungarian farmers themselves could end up losing part of their guaranteed domestic market the next time there is a good harvest. This could further increase both the uncertainty of their earnings from the market and their dependence on agricultural subsidies. Furthermore, fears of Ukrainian dumped prices do not seem entirely justified, since the price of corn is primarily determined by the global market, and not by Hungarians or Ukrainians; everyone sets their prices based on the prices quoted by the major stock exchanges. The processing industry also has other arguments to make, such as the fact that the fate of the domestic processing industry is important for the entire agricultural sector (since there is little domestic value-added production in agriculture, but a strong segment has developed in this area specifically). In fact, the issue may even extend beyond agriculture: biorefineries, and even biogas plants can help reduce the country’s dependence on energy imports. Meanwhile, of course, the entire European agricultural sector is relying on subsidies and the protection of markets; in other words, protecting the interests of local farmers is by no means a uniquely Hungarian phenomenon. If Hungary did not protect its farmers in an environment where everyone else does, it would indeed be impossible for them to survive. One way to address this would be to ensure that the subsidy system does not replace modernization, improving efficiency, and adapting to geographical conditions. The latter is particularly important in Hungary’s case, since climate change has been making it increasingly difficult to cultivate crops in certain areas while staying profitable. And if the farmers’ concern that Ukrainian grain will drive prices down is justified, then there needs to be some form of reasonable cross-subsidization. If imports drive the price down by 20 euros, that could amount to as much as 30 million euros in losses for farmers (20 times 1.5 million metric tons). Unfortunately, however, a shortage of raw materials leads to much bigger losses for processing companies, the dairy industry, feed manufacturers, livestock farming, bio-refineries, and isoglucose producers. Some kind of mechanism should definitely be found to avoid this, but there is no suitable method yet. The main reason for this is that Hungarian farmers are not satisfied with the current price either, and they feel that they cannot afford to go any lower. Although the current price of corn (80,000–87,000 forints per metric ton) is higher than last year’s (70,000 forints per metric ton), its cultivation is still unprofitable. Of course, if there are concerns about toxin contamination, they should be taken seriously. The problem, however, is that the doubts surrounding this issue were also part of a deliberately orchestrated political campaign. Until 2023, the Fidesz government had no concerns about the quality of Ukrainian corn. After the 2022 drought and the unprecedented levels of aflatoxin contamination, it was specifically Ukrainian corn which helped improve the Hungarian harvest. Concerns about the quality of Ukrainian corn over the past five years have not appeared to be well-founded at all; rather, they seemed to be nothing more than false fear-mongering. Would other EU countries with a high standard of food culture (Italy, Spain) allow risky raw materials into their markets? It’s unlikely, but on this too, let’s hear what the experts have to say! The main purpose of the European Commission’s RASFF food safety system is to enable Member State authorities to share information on food and feed safety risks with one another. The public RASFF database contains searchable notifications dating back to 2020, including for products from third countries. GMP+ International is the organization that operates the world’s leading nonprofit feed safety and sustainability certification system (the GMP+ Feed Certification Scheme). In 2026, Ukraine was classified as a country with a low aflatoxin risk with regard to corn production, while Hungary was classified as a country with a high aflatoxin risk. This classification is not set in stone, however; it is regularly reviewed based on weather conditions during harvest and laboratory monitoring results. At the beginning of the 2026/2027 harvest (in September 2026), for example, Ukraine’s classification was temporarily set to “medium risk” due to weather-related concerns, and then, following an evaluation of the October data, it was returned to the “low risk” category. The same October 2026 list classified Hungary as being “high risk.” Although this is not an official, government-issued classification, it is based on a significant amount of laboratory data.
